CALL TO THE PUBLIC:
Celia Laughlin, 2169 Hashknife Dr., Overgaard, stated that she is a P.C. and
represents one hundred twenty-five constituents.  She asked that an agenda item for
an Election Integrity Task Force Committee be on the next agenda. She requested
that they return to paper ballots and that all ballots from the 2022 Election be
preserved until the Task Force can complete an investigation.  She stated that there
is new evidence at the Supreme Court this week that the ES&S and the Dominion
machines have a way to get in the back door of the web mask.
Donna Sherwin, 1207 S. Forest Ln., Pinetop, stated that they need fair and safe
elections and to get rid of the machines, indicating that the machines are corrupt and
that there a ability to get into the machines with modems.   She stated that she
worked at the poll in Whiteriver, that a person came to vote, that she was told that
she had already voted, that she had the ballot she was mailed with her and that she
was angry that she couldn’t vote.  She stated that the elections need to be cleaned
up and to make it really simple by going back to paper ballots and a hand count. 
She indicated that they need to get rid of the machines and that if they aren’t going
to get rid of the machines, that need to let them know how they can clean them up
because they are not working to their benefit and that it’s not free and fair elections. 
She thanked Supervisor Whitesinger for hosting the town hall and all those that were
present at the town hall. She talked about having an agenda item, indicating that
they were told that to get on the agenda they needed to come to the meeting and
request it, that there were two people that were at the last meeting and that it was
still not on the agenda.  She talked about working together in the county and
indicated that we need free and fair elections for everybody, that nobody should be
denied their vote.
Belinda Quoq, 650 N. Penrod Rd., Show Low, stated that she is here to make the
Board aware of the immense distrust that the community has with the voting
process, indicating that there are inexcusable inconsistencies in the process that
opens doors to errors and criminal activity. She further stated that the right to vote is
the most important, valuable asset in ensuring true representation of government for
the future, indicating that the future is under attack and that the election process
should be at the top of the list to protect and ensure its security.  She talked about
flaws and vulnerabilities in the current election process, such as the system Eric
showing the voter rolls have over ninety-three percent of eligible residents that are
registered in Navajo County, which is thirty percent higher than the national
average; that four out of twenty-one precincts in Navajo County have no voters in
them; that drop boxes are left unsecured; conflicting information on how early ballots

them; that drop boxes are left unsecured; conflicting information on how early ballots
are processed; poll pads are connected to the internet controlled by third party

which opens the doors to a long list of vulnerabilities and there is no current

Jerry Hubbard, 2726 Covered Wagon Trail, Overgaard, addressed the Board
regarding ballot drop boxes in our county, indicating that the US Constitution
specifies that the times, places and manner of holding elections shall be prescribed
in each state by the legislature and that he is unable to find anything in ARS Section
16 that authorized or regulates the use of ballot drop boxes.  He stated that even if
the Election Procedure Manual describes the use of ballot drop boxes, they are not
in accordance with Arizona State Law and would be invalid.  He indicated that there
are many people who believe that drop boxes have no place in elections and that
there are two lawsuits regarding drop boxes being unconstitutional and illegal.  He
stated in 2005 the Commission of Federal Election Reform concluded that mail-in
ballots were a large source of potential election fraud.  He indicated that
unmonitored drop boxes increase the possibility for voter fraud by allowing
individuals to anonymously put ballots into the election system.  He stated that there
are seventeen drop box locations in Navajo County and talked about them being
purchased with a grant from The Center for Tech and Civic Life.  He spoke about the
drop boxes not having video monitoring.  He inquired how many Supervisors voted
in favor of them.
Chairman Whiting thanked those that came to speak on this issue.  He stated that
staff have been working on it and requested that Bryan Layton provide an update.
Bryan Layton stated that there is a lot of interest and questions about the election
process, how it works and voter integrity.  He indicated that the Board has directed
staff to investigate the community’s questions and concerns regarding elections and
to provide a report to the Board.  He stated that the report will include an overview of
the election process from start to finish and that their goal is to go through the
processes to provide more details and more transparency of the daily processes and
workflow.  He indicated that they want to have a productive and informative meeting
and that he believes that can be done if they identify and work with questions that
the residents have.  He stated that they have heard a few of the questions today and
that they want to understand the specific questions.  He further stated that there will
be a link of the county website today where residents can go in and identify
themselves, their party affiliation, and then submit their questions.  He indicated that
they have enlisted the help of the party leaderships and talked about the process
that will be used to be able to answer the questions of the citizens.  He stated that
this is a very important issue and that their plan is to come back to the second Board
meeting in April to provide a report.

b. Presentation and update on the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment
Program (BEAD) Challenge Process:
Grant Evans stated that in January the Board approved a contract with High
Street to help with the BEAD challenge process.  He indicated that the
consultants will present on what they have been doing to date as well as
some of the things moving forward.  He stated that they have been doing a
lot of mapping as well as data analysis and that they will show some of the
results from that.  He indicated that they have been working with the State
Broadband Office and the ACA over the past couple of months to make sure
this process aligns with the way the state is going to execute their program. 
He stated that they will cover in detail what is critical to the success of the
public outreach campaign that will launch today.  He further stated that there
are approximately 44,000 residences in Navajo County, off Tribal land, that
are currently broadband serviceable locations and that approximately 37,000
are not eligible to receive any of the funding but that the challenge process
provides an opportunity to take a deeper look into those areas and see if
there are inaccuracies or overstatement on the service level those residents
are getting.  He indicated that they will be sending postcards to the 37,000
residences and that public outreach is important to get the word to all
residents to be watching for the postcards and get educated about the
program.  He stated that they will be doing a press release and some social
media campaigns starting today to get the word out.  He advised that they
do have a BEAD Task Force in Navajo County, which consists of the partner
Cities and Towns and NPC.  He talked about the outreach that they have
done to date.   
Mark Eggy and Amy Link, with Highstreet, appearing virtual, showed a
presentation.  Mr. Eggy stated that the Federal Government is making an
investment in broadband infrastructure with the goal of connecting every
location in America to high-speed high quality broadband internet.  He talked
about the goal to maximize the broadband in Navajo County, indicating that
they want to make sure every eligible location is identified.  He stated that
there is approximately a billion dollars in funding for Arizona that will be
allocated to locations in priority locations that are unserved, underserved
and community institutions.  He stated that there are approximately 44,000
locations that can and should be connected, that 7,369 are currently eligible
for funding through the program and the remaining 37,000 are considered
ineligible.  He further stated that according to the national maps 32,000 of
those are considered to have access to high-speed internet and that the
additional 5,000 that are covered under the Rural Digital Opportunity grant
funding program that should establish high-speed access in the coming
years.  He indicated that there are four providers doing business in Navajo
County currently that are considered to meet federal standards for providing
qualifying high-speed high quality broadband internet, that some areas have
a choice between providers but that most locations only have one option. 
He stated that through this process part of their job is to make sure those
  
                                                                    4 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 10 -->
who don’t have a choice are still getting good service.  He reviewed all the
maps for different areas talking about the locations that show they are
covered, those that are not covered and those that are not included due to
being funded by other grants.  He talked about anchor institutions being
identified to make sure they are eligible for future funding.  He talked about
the challenge process, stating that the process allows an opportunity to
correct any inaccuracies in the State map.  He further talked about the
different kind of challenges: enforceable commitment, which is areas
covered by another grant; availability, which is when the provider reports
that high speed internet is available but the consumer is unable to subscribe;
speed, which is when consumers are able to subscribe but are unable to
obtain the advertised speeds and community anchor institutions, which are
missing entities that match state  CAI definition.  He stated that with the
community institutions any that are missing from the map can be added to
statewide funding so that in the final stages of the grom they would be
eligible if there is money left after all of the unserved and underserved
locations are connected.  
Ms. Link talked about the outreach and engagement, indicating that they will
be sending out postcards to 37,000 locations to verify they have the
high-speed internet or that they are able to receive it.  She talked about
postcards, stating that you can either scan the QR code or go to the
website.  She indicated that they want everyone on the same website and
that from there it will direct everyone according to the type of challenge to
make it as easy as possible.  She talked about the website, the information
that it will provide, and the options provided depending on the type of
challenge that applies to the location.  She stated that for the speed
challenge they will have to take the test three times on different days to
make sure it’s an accurate representation of the performance.  She talked
about the need to get the word out, the press release that will be done, the
social media posts, and advised that the post cards will start arriving about a
week from today.  She stated that you don’t have to have a post card to
respond, that you can just go to the website.  She reviewed the timeline for
the challenge process, indicating that they need all of the information to be
collected by May 15, 2024.  She stated that they would like to have
everyone start as soon as possible due to having the three-day time period
for doing the speed challenge.  She further stated that they hope to be able
to track where they get the responses from so they can do some additional
follow-up for the areas with a low response. 
Supervisor Whitesinger inquired if the website is active now and how those
who are having issues with internet would be able to access the website?
Mr. Evans stated that the website is live.  He further stated that if the areas
where they are having issues to connect are already known, they are
already eligible for funding, but that if their property is being overstated, they
will need a speed test to correct that and that the speed test will have to be
taken at the address to validate it. 
A discussion was held regarding how to get people to participate in the
challenge process that has internet but that it is slow or limited. 
Vice-Chairwoman Benally inquired if this is just for those with internet,
indicating that in the northern part of District One there are individuals
without internet or are in blackout areas.
Mr. Evans stated that would be part of the availability challenge, indicating if

SHERIFF'S OFFICE:
 
a. Consideration of an agreement between the Department of Public Safety
and Navajo County Sheriff's Office and Navajo County regarding local
border support:
Sheriff David Clouse stated that the Border Strike Force was initiated by
Governor Ducey approximately nine or ten years ago, which was a fund that
legislature funded through the Department of Public Safety that was opened
to a couple of Sheriff’s Office, mainly the four border counties and then
extended to Yavapai County. He talked about the Navajo County K9
program being top notch statewide and that they are always looking for ways
to attach to it.  He indicated that the program is funded through general fund
money at the County, which causes some decisions when determining
where to put resources, but that they choose to continue it because they are
productive, have had lots of results and it serves the community well.  He
stated that the Local Border Support Fund that Governor Hobbs started and
that it is local government, state government, and a bipartisan effort that is
serving all of its constituents.  He talked about how Navajo County is eligible
for so many of the border grants, indicating that they are interdicting a lot of
the drugs that leave Arizona and go out to the rest of the country on I-40,
that through the stats they found sixty percent of all fentanyl seized is in
Arizona, and that a lot of those in custody housed in the jail stem from these
types of crimes.  He indicated that there is a big impact on the budget and
that it was costing four to five hundred thousand in detention costs every
year.  He talked about an incident with an inmate bringing in contraband into
the jail, sharing it with cellmates and the cost that was incurred for medical. 
He indicated that these small scenarios indicate they need more funding and
support as they combat these things.  He talked about the border issues
being a crisis and how it impacts the small counties, hospitals, and schools. 
 He talked about how the Sheriff’s Association asked that Governor Hobbs
not do away with the Board Strike Force, that part of her agenda was to
disband it but that she decided to change it to a local border support where
local agencies can use it for enforcement needs.  He addressed the amount
of funds that Navajo County is eligible to receive and stated that a lot of it will
be used for personnel, indicating that four Navajo County employees would
be funded at seventy-five percent, five of the Navajo County municipal
agencies at seventy-five percent and two from the County Attorney’s Office
that prosecute these crimes at fifty percent and that the remaining funds
would be for the aviation unit.  He talked about the long history of MCAT in
Navajo County, indicating that they’ve been one of the best assets for pro
active law enforcement within the county.  He indicated that this task force
has been a great asset to work on the high crime areas, the more
sophisticated types of cases and being able to focus on dismantling a lot of

National Healthcare Decisions Day, Public Health Week, World
Immunization Week and National Infant Immunization Week, Minority Health
Month, Alcohol Awareness Month, Autism Acceptance Month, Donate Life
Month, Nation Child Abuse Prevention Month, and the Month of the Young

Supervisor Seymore made a motion to approve a proclamation,
proclaiming April 2024 as "Public Health Month in Navajo County", motion

Supervisor Peshlakai made a motion to return to regular session, motion
seconded by Supervisor Whitesinger.  Vote unanimous approving the

PUBLIC WORKS:
 
a. Consideration of award of contract #B24-02-006 Supply of Various Roadway
Materials to Brimhall Sand, Rock & Building Materials, Hatch Construction &
Paving, Inc., Perkins Aggregates, Inc., Perkins Cinders, Inc. and
Schuck Development effective March 28, 2024 :
Madhav Mundle stated that Public Works uses this contract to procure
various types of materials to maintain roadways and other related activities. 
He indicated that they like to have multiple contracts to ensure availability of
materials for covered based on pricing, quality of materials and location.  He
talked about the bid process, indicating that the details are in the packet.  He
stated that staff recommends approval as to all bidders.
Vice-Chairwoman Benally made a motion to approve award of contract
#B24-02-006 Supply of Various Roadway Materials to Brimhall Sand, Rock
& Building Materials, Hatch Construction & Paving, Inc., Perkins Aggregates,
Inc., Perkins Cinders, Inc. and Schuck Development effective March 28,
2024, motion seconded by Supervisor Seymore.  Vote unanimous
approving the motion. 
 
  
PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT: 
 
1. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution
Number 14-2024, approving/denying text amendment to Article 25, Section
2521, regarding wireless communication facilities:
Cody Cooper stated that last year Planning and Development brought forth
the initial wireless communications ordinance within the zoning ordinance. 
He indicated that since then they have had twelve cell towers in front of the
Board, that they have looked at it and analyze the ordinance to see what is
working and what isn’t and be able to bring it back with some
recommendations for changes.  He talked about the proposed amendments
they would like to make to the resolution, including striking the two-foot
horizontal to one-foot vertical waiver for residentially designed properties;
  
                                                                    8 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 14 -->
striking the application requirement for complying with federal standards;
striking the application requirement for notifying the appropriate agencies
within the vicinity; and adding in the facilities as permitted uses for all
governmental agencies.  He stated that staff is recommending approval and
that the Planning & Zoning Commission unanimously recommended
approval last month.  He advised that as of today they have not received any
public comments.    
Chairman Whiting opened the meeting for public comment.  There being
no comments, the public hearing was closed.
 
Supervisor Seymore stated that he thinks this is something that will help in
the process.  He shared his appreciation to staff for looking through this and
finding the common ground on things that don’t need to be revisited every
time.  He stated that he appreciates the efforts of staff and the
Commissioners.
Chairman Whiting shared his appreciation to the team for working on this.
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
14-2024, approving text amendment to Article 25, Section 2521, regarding
wireless communication facilities, motion seconded
by Vice-Chairwoman Benally.  Vote unanimous approving the motion. 
 
2. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution
Number 15-2024, approving/denying a Special Use Permit to allow for the
construction of a 199' monopole wireless communication tower and
associated facilities located in the Clay Springs area:
Tyler Richards stated that this is for a cell tower south of the Clay Springs
area.  He talked about the height of tower and the location, indicating that it
is 49.48 acres and is zoned A-General, which is non-residential.  He
reviewed the project description, stating that it will be one wireless
communication tower and associated facilities, it will be located 1199 feet
from all property boundaries, that it will be at fifty-by-fifty compound
surrounded by an eight-foot chain link fence.  He talked about the site plan
with location of tower and the details of the tower.  He provided photos of the
location with sim views.  He stated that the applicant held a citizen
participation meeting, that one person attended and was in favor of the
tower.  He further stated that they received one letter from a citizen stating
some concerns regarding the location of the tower, that staff did reach out to
them and that a lot of their concerns were alleviated.  She advised that this
has been noticed and posted in compliance with state law in the ordinance. 
He stated that this is in compliance with the comprehensive plan and that it’s
compatible with current and likely future uses of the property.  He stated that
staff, as well as the Planning and Zoning Commission, recommend
approval.   
 
Chairman Whiting opened the meeting for public comments.  There being
no comments, the public hearing was closed.
Supervisor Seymore made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
15-24, approving a Special Use Permit to allow for the construction of a 199'

monopole wireless communication tower and associated facilities located in
the Clay Springs area, motion seconded by Supervisor Whitesinger.  Vote
unanimous approving the motion. 
 
3. Presentation regarding the ongoing update to the Navajo County
Comprehensive Plan being conducted by Logan Simpson Design and
Navajo County Planning and Development Services Staff:
Cody Cooper stated that last year Planning and Development went out for
an RFP for a full update of their comprehensive plan, indicating that they
have only had limited updates since 2004.  He further stated that Logan
Simpson Design was selected, and he talked about the work they have been
doing to date.
Terry Hogan, Project Manager with Logan Simpson Design, talked the
Consultant team consisting of individuals from Logan Simpson as the Lead
Consultant, Kimley Horn to support Transportation and Water Resources
and Elliot D. Pollack and Company to support Housing and Economic
Growth and the Navajo County team.  She stated that Comprehensive Plans
are required for all Arizona counties according to Title 11 and that they are
required to have certain elements and topics as well as public involvement
and that they must be adopted or readopted every ten years.  She indicated
that the Navajo County plan is in conformance with statute since it has been
readopted over the years, but that it hasn’t had any major updates since the
original adoption in 2004.  She stated that the purpose of the plan is to guide
the adjusted harmonious development of the area pursuant to present and
future needs, to conserve natural resources of the county, ensure efficient
expenditure of public monies and to promote public health, safety, and
welfare.  She reviewed the planning hierarchy pyramid, stating that the
comprehensive plan is the foundation of all planning tools and that as you go
up the pyramid you get more specific in your regulations or plans.  She
talked about the topics that will be covered, stating that the statute requires
all comprehensive plans include foundational elements of land use and
transportation and that as population increases over 125,000 there are more
required elements.  She talked about the future land use map that the
county currently has, stating that it shows future land use designations of
what the community has aspired for the area to look like in the future.  She
further talked about the process for determining goals and policies and the
implementation plan.  She reviewed the project schedule, indicating that it is
a twelve-month process.  She stated that the public engagement process
started in February and will go through December to allow for the community
input of whether they are hitting the mark or not.  She indicated that at the
end of the adopting plan process there will be a sixty-day review where they
will send the draft plan to everyone that has been involved in the process for
comments and then they will come back through process prior to going to
the Board for final adoption.  She talked about where they are in the process
currently and the work that they are currently doing.  She reviewed the
engagement strategies for public participation, which is required by statute,
indicating that they will have opportunity for written comment, public
hearings with effective notes and open discussions, communications,
dialogues, and consideration of the public comments. She talked about the
project branding, indicating that they are following the style guide.  She
further talked about the Comprehensive Plan Commission, which consists of
  
                                                                    10 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 16 -->
entities from the federal level, the state level and different county entities and
departments, noting that they will meet three times during the process.  She
stated that they will be doing community meetings or community interviews,
which will be one on ones or focus groups, stating that they work working on
getting contacts for different entities and that if there is any interest in being
a part of this, they can contact Cody Cooper.  She indicated that they want
as much input as possible for this plan and that they will be holding different
meetings.  She stated that they will be providing updates to the Planning
Commission and the Board through the process.  She indicated that the
project website is up and talked about the information that will be on the
website, as well as other outreach strategies.  She reviewed the next steps
and what will be done over the next several months.         
Supervisor Whitesinger shared her appreciation to Public Works and all of
those involved in getting this going.  She stated that she is looking forward to
participating in the conversations.  She talked about being able to see the
growth in the organization to best be able to support the communities and
those who request support from the organization.     
Supervisor Seymore shared his appreciation for the presentation and the
energy and time put into it.  He stated one of the biggest things we have as a
community is the land, the land preservation and the development and
growth of it.  He talked about being able to have a map going forward and
about being able to create a vision.  He stated that this is a great
perspective and that it will help as Navajo County expands and grows in the
future.  He thanked all of those that have been involved in the process.   
 
COUNTY BUSINESS UPDATE: Report from County Manager, County Attorney and
Board members :
Bryan talked about complex rehabilitation that is going on, indicating that this will
preserve the building for continued use and that the repairs are needed repairs.  He
indicated that the contractors are doing their best not to be too noisy during working
hours and that they are excited to have it completed in the next couple of months. 
He talked about budget meetings, indicating that they have completed the
department meetings.  He talked about the teamwork and collaboration with
departments, stating that it has been a pleasure working with them and that it is
encouraging that they are concerned with all of Navajo County and not just their
departments.  He stated that the Finance Department is working on a base budget
and will be presenting to the Board in the next couple of weeks.
Supervisor Seymore talked about this being a special time of year with Easter,
indicating that it brings hope, peace, and reverence of the true meanings of his belief
of Easter which is the hope of life going forward.  He talked about an Easter lily that
is blooming in yard while everything else is completely dead.  He stated that there is
always hope, that he is grateful for the support of the communities, staff, and the
Board.  He stated that he looks forward to being able to work and be a part of the
community as they develop Navajo County.
Supervisor Peshlakai reported on attending as many of the ten Chapter Meetings
in his district.  He talked about the Community Network Meeting that they held in
Hardrock, indicating that they have started going to the communities again this year
to connect with them.  He addressed about the agenda that they had at the last
meeting.  He talked on the Community cleanups that they will be working to partner
on.  He stated that this is the 12 th year that they have been doing the Community
Meetings, indicating that former Supervisor Thompson started them, and that Nicole
                                                                    11 of 13 
DRAFT

<!-- page 17 -->
Reske has been successful in connecting with different resources to participate in
the meetings.  He talked about the Navajo Nation Improvement Transportation
Meeting that he participated in.  He talked about participating in the Hopi Tribal
Council’s second quarter session, indicating that they were able to provide an
introduction and give a brief overview of the programs and services available.
Supervisor Whitesinger reported on attending the White Mountain Business
Roundtable where Grant Evans shared a presentation regarding the work being
done on broadband and she shared her appreciation to Mr. Evans.  She stated that
part of that was also a presentation from the townships and indicated that one of the
things of concern for the communities and the investment of work that the
communities do to help in economic growth or partnerships.  She stated that there
has been a lot of conversations in the way of transportation, economic growth, and
future opportunities. She stated that she has a White Mountain Regional
Transportation Committee Meeting and that she is looking forward to the
conversations to continue to prioritize the needs of the local region and to be able to
advocate for the priorities.    
Vice-Chairwoman Benally reported on attending Chapter meetings on the
Navajo Nation level, as well as the Winslow City Council meetings.  She talked
about working with NDOT and the BIA on graveling projects, indicating that they are
moving slowly, that they should be starting again this week so they can move
forward on the two projects.  She indicated that tomorrow is the Grand Opening of
the N71 where they completed the pavement and requested that an official from
Public Works be present, if possible, to represent the County.  She stated that this
will make the roads more accessible and will help the school by making travelling to
the schools easier.   She talked about the impact that the weather has on the
roads.   She addressed the new building for NPC that will be in Kayenta, stating that
they are looking forward to having it and that it will allow for more students to attend
college there since it will be a bigger building.  She reported on attending the Tribal
Delegation Meeting in Hopi yesterday and thanked those that were able to attend. 
She stated that the Chapters are getting prepared for Earth Day cleanups in April,
indicating that they have been requesting clean up kits from Public Works and that
they are working with them so they can start that.  She noted that some of the
Townships have already started and have been collecting trash over the past couple
of weeks. 
Chairman Whiting reported on attending the Aztec Land and Cattle Board Meeting,
indicating that they have been great partners and that it was an honor to speak with
them regarding the partnership.  He thanked Bryan Layton for the update on
Elections and for providing the information on the link that is live on the website.  He
thanked the Party Chairs for partnering on the that and the Elections staff for working
on a presentation.  He wished everyone a Happy Easter with their family, friends,
and loved ones.

Title: 2024 Misdemeanor Contract - David Moore
Submitted For: Brad Carlyon, County Attorney  Submitted By: Lynda Young, Office Manager
Department: County Attorney
Motion before the Board:
Award of the Navajo County Legal Services Contract B24-01-009 to Moore Law, PLLC
Background:
Until Attorney I position is filled, we will contract legal prosecuting services to cover the Show Low and
Pinetop-Lakeside Justice Courts.  
Fiscal Impact
Fiscal Year: FY24
Budgeted Y/N: Y
Amount Requested:
Fiscal Impact:
$1,300 per week to cover two justice courts.
Attachments
2024 Misdemeanor Contract David Moore 
Form Review
Inbox Reviewed By Date
County Attorney Melissa Buckley 03/27/2024 09:27 AM
Lynda Young (Originator) Lynda Young 03/29/2024 11:44 AM

<!-- page 535 -->
CONTRACT FOR PROFESSIONAL SERVICES 
AGREEMENT made as of March 26, 2024 , 2024, between Navajo County 
("County") and Moore Law, PLLC ("Consultant"). 
WHEREAS, County requires certain professional services for Navajo County Legal 
Services, Contract No. B24-01-009 ("Project"); and 
WHEREAS, Consultant represents that it has the necessary expertise to provide such 
services in accordance with the terms of this Agreement. 
NOW, THEREFORE, the parties agree as follows: 
1. Services. Consultant shall perform the work described in the Proposal dated
February 15, 2024 and those additional items set forth in the Consultant's Fee
Proposal dated 3-27-24 , 2024, in a competent and professional manner
to the satisfaction of County. The Consultant's Proposal and Fee Proposal is attached
hereto and by this reference incorporated herein.
2. Contract Documents. The Contract Documents comprise this Contract, Request for
Qualifications No. B24-01-009, Fee Proposal dated 3-27-24 , 2024,
Consultant's Proposal Submittal dated February 15, 2024, and addendums thereto, if
any. If any incorporated term is inconsistent with the Contract, this Contract shall
control over all others; the Request for Qualifications shall control over the
Consultants proposal.
3. Consultant's Expertise. Consultant warrants that it has the ability, authority,
capacity and professional expertise to perform this Agreement. Consultant shall
provide an adequate staff of experienced personnel, capable of and devoted to the
successful accomplishment of the work to be performed hereunder. Consultant shall
assign specific individuals to key positions. Once assigned to work under this
Agreement, key personnel shall not be removed or replaced without County's prior
written approval.
4. Independent Contractor. Consultant acknowledges that it is an independent

Narrative 
Please structure your proposal to provide the following information in the order indicated.  Provide the narrative in 
paragraph form in the text field provided.  Please be thorough but strive for brevity. 
1. Briefly describe your organization’s history, mission and goals. 
Timber Mesa Fire and Medical District (TMFMD) was formed in 2014 with the consolidation of the Show Low, Lakeside, 
and Linden Fire Districts. In 2018 TMFMD grew again when we were asked to consolidate the White Mountain Lake Fire 
District, adding 40 square miles to our service area. TMFMD is a career emergency service organization operating out of 
5 stations, with 112 employees, and covers 216 square miles in the communities of the White Mountains in South 
Navajo County. 
In 2018 TMFMD was also awarded an ambulance service area by AZDHS. TMFMD initially applied for 216 square miles of 
service area to cover our district's residence. After the AZDHS Director review our case, she felt that TMFMD was better 
equipped to serve not only our citizens but also the rural and wilderness areas around us. The result of that decision was 
TMFMD being awarded a 440 square mile ambulance service area bordered by White Mountain Apache Tribe to the 
South, Heber/Overgaard to the West, Taylor/Snowflake to the North, and Vernon to the East. 
Mission: Deliver excellent service to our community through empathy, empowerment, and professionalism. 
2020/2023 Strategic Goals: Strengthening Partnerships and Agreements, Employee Relations and Retention, 
Providing and Maintaining Adequate Staffing and Service Levels, Expand and Improve Medical Services, Providing 
Training to Meet the Needs of the Organization and the Community, Providing and Maintaining Facilities Adequate for 
the Organization, Services and the Community, Develop and Implement an Apparatus and Vehicle Replacement Program 
to meet the needs of the Services and the organization, Developing the Code Enforcement Program to Meet the Needs 
of the Community and Provide for Improved Life Safety and Maintaining and Improving the Community Risk Reduction 
Program to Ensure a Safer Community 
2. To determine eligibility for this grant, if the applying organization is non-municipal or non-profit, please describe 
your relationship with the supporting municipality, how this project will benefit the municipality, and the 
municipality’s role in this project, if applicable.  If the applying organization is a municipality or a municipal sub-
division please enter the text “Not applicable” and go to item 3. 
TMFMD is a special taxing district as allowed by Arizona Law under Title 48. TMFMD is a governmental agency but is not 
under the direction of a municipality or County Board of Supervisors but instead reports to an elected Fire Board. 
TMFMD does cover the City of Show Low, part of the Town of Pinetop/Lakeside, and a large area of unincorporated 
Navajo County. TMFMD is an active partner with Navajo County in many projects. TMFMD also works with The County in

<!-- page 547 -->
Gila River Indian Community Grant Application 
Grant Cycle 2024 
 
4 
 
providing trainings to county employees, assisting The County Emergency Operations personnel in the deployment of 
large scale training exercises that include area law enforcement and fire agencies and assists The County with annual 
Point of Distribution (POD) exercises, to name a few examples. TMFMD enjoys a robust relationship with Navajo County 
and with all governments listed above and all our other regional partners. 
3. Describe the proposed project, objectives, and your plan to implement. 
TMFMD is in need 103 new radios to outfit our emergency vehicles and employees. We have taken a phased approach 
to accomplish the goal. We have been able to budget approx. $10,000 a year for radio replacement, however, this does 
not come close to meeting our need. Prior to purchasing the BKR-5000 radios, we were using the BK-150 radios. The 
issue is two fold; the BK-150 was discontinued by the manufacturer, severely limiting our ability to replace damaged or 
old units, as well as making service for these radios very difficult. We, therefore, were forced to look at other radio 
options. The Motorola radios were enticing, however their cost far outwayed our ability to purchase. The BKR 5000 
however, met all of our requirements and fit within a tighter budget. These new BKR-5000 radios are both P25 and NFPA 
compliant and meet are needs for emergency communications. 
In FY22/23 we were able to purchase a total of 7 new BKR-5000 radios, severely short of the over all need. Our total 
need was 110 radios, the purchase of the last 7 brought our need to 103 at a cost of $206,660.23 before tax. We plan to 
use this award to continue our phased approach by purchasing close to half the radios we need and then following this 
grant award up with a submission in FY25 for the remainder of the need.  
Upon award, we will reach out to our vendors and purchase 45 new BKR-radios utilizing our current internal 
procurement policy. These 45 radios will completely outfit our first out units including 4 fire engines, 10 ambulances, 
and three command vehicles. Each unit will receive enough radios for the staff that respond on them with vehicle 
chargers, batteries, and microphones. We will be able to provide GRIC with the total calls for service that these radios 
have been used on after a year of service.  
4. Describe how the proposed project satisfies one or more of the priority funding areas identified by the Gila River 
Indian Community. 
The BKR-5000 radio request directly matches the GRIC grant priotirites of Healthcare and Public Safety. TMFMD provides 
medical care on thousands of incidents each year. EMS is the first line of medical response for patients needing medical 
care. EMS provides the emergent health care for individuals facing emergent medical issues. As defined, TMFMD is a 
Public Safety organization providing fire and medical services to our communities and those communities around us. 
Communications are a vital tool used in handling emergency situations and provides for efficient communcications with

<!-- page 548 -->
Gila River Indian Community Grant Application 
Grant Cycle 2024 
 
5 
 
dispatch, other responding agencies, and other units within the district. Additionally, dependable communications are 
vital for responder safety providing them a clear line of communication with the support they need to provide service to 
the community.  
5. Identify the needs/problems to be addressed, target population and number of people to be served by the 
project. 
The need to be addressed stems from the need for funding for the purchase of critical equipment. Fire districts in 
Arizona are limited in several ways with respect to their funding sources. We are the only taxing entity in Arizona that 
has a hard rate cap. Our budgeted levy growth is limited to 8% annually and the Limited Property Value (LPV) for each 
individual property is limited to no more than 5% growth per year. This last limitation (5% LPV growth) was the most 
recently established, and perhaps the most devastating. The voters approved Prop. 117 which limited the taxable value 
growth on real property to 5% annually. The values were originally indexed to the bottom of the market during the most 
recent recession. In that recession, Timber Mesa Fire and Medical District lost approximately 38% of its taxable value 
between 2010 and 2015; with the new limitation in place, it will take us until 2025 (at least) to recover to 2008 taxable 
property values. Per Navajo County Assessor's office, today the LPV of the properties in the District is still 9.1% below 
what the value was in 2009. The current political legislative changes (capping levy limits), have resulted in growth 
demands and budgetary limitations which have exceeded our organizations' ability to appropriately address this project. 
The current budget and subsequent budgets will provide for sustainability at current staffing levels but have limited 
ability to address the need for capital equipment and provide very little margin for funding equipment needs at a rate 
needed to keep up with applicable equipment standards. TMFMD does not have the financial capacity to fund additional 
capital projects and sustain funding for staffing and maintain response units with all the District needs. Due to these 
mentioned circumstances, TMFMD has sought to obtain funding elsewhere (i.e. state assistance programs or other grant 
programs), we have restructured debt service, controlled expenditures, developed a capital replacement plan, 
implemented non-tax revenue streams, and applied for grants to balance the budget and address financial impacts. 
Additionally, there have been two recent initiatives that attempted to secure additional funding. Prop. 428, Timber 
Mesa Capital Bond for $18M was attempted in 2021, and Prop. 310 Statewide sales tax to fund fire districts was 
attempted in 2022 and both have failed at the ballot box. 
6. Define the project as a new or continuing program.  Has GRIC previously funded this project?

<!-- page 549 -->
Gila River Indian Community Grant Application

6 
 
This is a continuing project for TMFMD as we have purcahased 7 new radios in the past few years. However, we are 
struggling to find the financial resources to purchase enough P25 compliant radios for the amount of firefighters that 
operate within our district on a daily basis. This is a continuing project for TMFMD, however, it is a new request for GRIC.   
7. Provide a brief timeline including start and finish dates.  Indicate if the timeline is flexible. 
If funded, we would immediiatley seek the approval of both the Navajo County Board of Supervisors as well as the 
TMFMD Governing Board to accept the grant and to move forward with the purchase. Within the first 3 months of 
approval we would seek quotes as per our internal policy. The equipment would be ordered based on best value. 
Depending on manufacturer lead times, we should take receipt of the equipment within the first 6 months of approval. 
Once all equipment was received we would install the equipment in our vehicles and provide necessary training for all 
effected personnel. This timeline is flexible based on manufacturing lead times and availability.  
8. Identify other organizations, partners or funders participating in the project and their roles. 
TMFMD would be the direct recipient of the grant funds and subsequent equipment. We would work with Arizona based 
vendors (if available) to request quotes. Our mutual aid partners would benefit indirectly as we operate with these 
organizations on a consistent basis. These communities include Show Low, Linden, Lakeside, White Mountain Lakes, 
Pinetop, White Mountain Apache Tribe, Heber, Overgaard, Taylor, Snowflake, Vernon, Concho, and many others. 
9. Would you be able to implement the proposed plan if your organization received partial funding for this project? 
Yes. We would be able to purchase a limited number of radios based on a partial funding. We would pursue other grant 
funding opportunities in 2025 if necessary.  
10. Describe your plan for project financial sustainability beyond the grant period.  If this is a program/project 
previously funded by the Gila River Indian Community describe efforts made towards the previously described 
sustainability plan. 
TMFMD operates under a comprehensive 2-year strategic plan that includes a capital replacement plan. This plan is 
developed with input from community partners and members of the public to help determine the priorities for spending 
and replacement. This plan outlines details for spreading out the purchase of new equipment and provides TMFMD with 
the ability to plan and prepare for the purchase of replacement equipment. After the purchase of the proposed 
equipment, TMFMD would update it's capital replacement plan to include the equipment provided. TMFMD is working

<!-- page 550 -->

7 
 
to identify alternative funding sources as was indicated above in the bond that was proposed to the voters but failed. 
Additionally, TMFMD is progressive by forecasting our spending needs to provide for financial sustainability. 
11. Describe your plan to document progress and results. 
Each step of the plan outlined above is part of TMFMD's internal procrument process. Starting with board approval, 
which is public record and documented as such, we would then complete the procurement process based on internal 
policy. Call data associated with the equipment is tracked in our incident management software which captures each 
and every response that the requested equipment would respond on.

separate attachment, please indicate that here. 
No other tribal awards outside of Gila River have been awarded to TMFMD at any time. TMFMD did apply for a Tohono 
O’Odham Nation Prop 202 grant in 2023, we were not awarded through that process.

 Project Budget Detail 
Please provide a narrative description for each of the project budget items listed on the previous page.  Include the 
dollar figure and how it was derived. 
1. The BKR5000-T3BS-1 is a 6-watt, 5000 channel, digital and analog VHF portable (hand-held) radio. The district has 
been slowly converting our old, outdated, discontinued, and non NFPA and P25 compliant radios. However, due to the 
expense associated with the radios, the constant need of replacement due to damage and use, and the ever growing 
need to outfit our fleet, we are unable to keep up with the need. The cost per radio is $1,404.55 each. We are seeking 45 
radios (less than half of the 103 total need) which brings us to the total budget of $63,204.75 with a 10% match from our 
capital replacement budget.  
2. The BKR uses a BKR0101 4900 MAH LI-ION battery. We are requesting one battery for each radio. The cost is $147 for 
each battery, with a match of 10%, the total cost for 45 batteries is $6,615.00. 
3. Each radio requires an antenna for its operation. We are requesting 45 antennas at a cost of $47.59 each. With the 
10% match that makes he total cost of 45 antennas $2,141.55. 
4. The microphone is designed to clip on to an article of clothing or PPE allowing the radio to be secured on the belt or in 
a pocket while being used. The microphone also improves the ability to hear the radio when it is stored away from the 
users ear. The cost of the microphone is $225 each with a toal caost after the 10% match of $10,125.00. 
5. The ECIM-BK3 vehicle charger has two functions. It charges the batteries of the radio as well as provides a secure 
mount for the radio when not in use. Each radio needs a charger and each charger costs $148.80. With the 10% match 
the total cost for th chargers is $6,696.00.  
6. Tax is set at 8.43%. We are able to provide a 10% match for a total of $7,484.35.

March 22, 2024 
 
 
 
The Honorable Mark Kelly 
U.S. Senate 
516 Hart Senate Office Building 
Washington, DC 20510 
 
Re: Timber Mesa Fire and Medical District application for FY25 Congressional Spending Grant 
 
Dear Senator Kelly, 
 
The Navajo County Board of Supervisors is in support of the Timber Mesa Fire and Medical 
District’s grant application requesting funds for three (3) ambulances and two (2) support 
vehicles.  
 
The importance of adding these vehicles due to the increasing call volumes, both emergent and 
non-emergent, is critical to our communities. We understand that Timber Mesa Fire and Medical 
District continues to see a steep increase in mileage put on the current ambulances. Timber Mesa 
Fire and Medical District has transported over 1100 patients to hospitals off the mountain 
(Phoenix, Tucson, Flagstaff) from Summit Regional Medical Center in just the last 2 years. 
These inter-facilities are vital in caring for area residents and visitors as they require specialized 
care not currently available at Summit Regional Medical Center.   
 
Although Timber Mesa Fire and Medical District can replace ambulances at a rate that can 
sustain the fleet, they are struggling to keep up with the mileage placed on these ambulances due 
to frequent high-mileage transports. As an example, the 2020 ambulance that serves the 
downtown Show Low area has almost 200,000 miles on it currently.  
 
We support the use of these two (2) support vehicles to train our area partners and community, 
tow our wildland response UTV and other various trailers, and support emergency operations in 
the field.  
 
We respectfully request that the Timber Mesa Fire Medical District’s grant application request 
be given your full and fair consideration. 
 
Sincerely,  
 
Jason Whiting, Chairman 
Navajo County Board of Supervisors

RESOLUTION  -24 
 
A RESOLUTION OF THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OF NAVAJO COUNTY 
REAFFIRMING THE COUNTY’S FAIR HOUSING POLICY, MAKING KNOWN ITS 
COMMITMENT TO THE PRINCIPLE OF FAIR HOUSING AND DESCRIBING 
ACTIONS IT SHALL UNDERTAKE TO AFFIRMATIVELY FURTHER FAIR 
HOUSING 
 
 
HEREAS, the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 as amended 
requires that all applicants for Community Development Block Grant funds certify 
that they shall affirmatively further fair housing; and 
 
 
HEREAS, the Civil Rights Act of 1968 (commonly known as the Federal Fair 
Housing Act) and the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 declare a national  
policy to prohibit discrimination in the sale, rental, leasing and financing of housing  
or land to be used for the construction of housing or in the provision of brokerage 
services, on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national 
origin; and 
 
 
HEREAS, fairness is the foundation of the American system and reflects traditional 
American values; and 
 
 
 
HEREAS, discriminatory housing practices undermine the strength and vitality of 
America and its people; 
 
 
 
OW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Board of Supervisors of Navajo 
County hereby wish all persons living, working, doing business in or traveling through 
this county to know that: 
 
Discrimination in the sale, rental, leasing and financing of housing or land to be used for 
construction of housing, or in the provision of brokerage services on the basis of race, 
color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status or national origin is prohibited by Title VIII 
of the Fair Housing Act Amendments of 1988; and that it is the policy of Navajo County 
to implement programs, within the constraints of its resources, to ensure equal 
opportunity in housing for all persons regardless of race, color, religion, sex, handicap, 
familial status or national origin; and within available resources, Navajo County will

Dear Mr. Mundle: 
 
Wilson & Company, Inc., Engineers & Architects (Wilson & Company) is pleased to submit this 
Contract Modification #2 proposal to provide the additional scope, schedule, and cost estimate to 
provide professional engineering services and consulting services to prepare complete the 
environmental compliance for the Joseph City School Route, Sidewalk & Crosswalk 
Improvements project funded by a Community Development Block Grant and additionally, the 
Arizona Transportation Alternatives Grant.  
 
Thank you very much for this opportunity to expand the project limits and continue working with 
you on this project. We are confident you will be pleased with the quality, timeliness, and 
responsiveness of our services and work documents. 
 
PROJECT LOCATION AND LIMITS 
 
Joseph City is an unincorporated community located in Navajo County, Arizona. It is located along 
Interstate 40 approximately eighty miles east of Flagstaff and ten miles west of Holbrook. Joseph 
City recorded a population of 1,908 inhabitants in 2020 according to the U.S. Census Bureau. 
 
The proposed project limits are shown below within the orange boundary depicted below in Figure 
1. The project will provide recommended improvements to enhance the pedestrian circulation 
between the two schools, Joseph City Elementary School, and Joseph City JR/SR High School) and 
improve pedestrian crossings at specified locations.

Figure 1 - Project Area 
 
SCOPE OF WORK 
Wilson & Company will perform the professional services required to prepare the necessary 
environmental documentation to obtain clearance for construction. 
 
Environmental tasks required to complete a Categorical Exclusion will be required for NEPA 
certification under the direction of the lead agency, the Arizona Department of Transportation.  
 
Resource studies including desktop assessments of cultural and biological resources will be 
completed.  
 
Studies for Hazardous Materials (HazMat) will be conducted by subcontractor Ninyo & Moore. 
(See attached Scope of Work for these services) 
 
Studies will be conducted in an approximate 1100-acre location, although the APE is recognized to 
cover approximately 30 acres. A limited number of checks on known natural and cultural resources 
in the project area will be completed. 
 
A Biological Evaluation will be required and a Class I background review of historic properties 
within a half mile of the APE with a focus on the built environment will be required.  
 
No Historical In-Use Structure Forms will be required. A 4(f) assessment will be required and 
included in the cultural report.  
 
Wilson & Company will draft the agency cultural consultation letters and address no more than one 
round of comments.  
 
ADOT will complete a Categorical Exclusion, 4(f) letters, and Environmental Clearance in-house. A 
HazMat summary report that includes results of testing for lead, asbestos, and a PISA will be 
conducted by sub-consultant Ninyo & Moore.  No Clean Water Act permitting, Air Quality, or 
Noise assessments are anticipated. Only one round of comments will be required for the 
environmental assessment documents and one round of comments from consultation. No ASM

registration or curation fees will be required. A cultural records search of the ASM’s ARO will be 
required. No cultural or biological fieldwork will be required. No more than 3 in-use historic 
structures and no more than 12 historic properties will be identified in the Class I.  
 
All deliverables will be submitted electronically. No more than 3 external project/team meetings are 
anticipated.  
 
Any additional work beyond these assumptions would require a change-order request. 
 
Based on the information above the following attached scopes of work and fee breakdowns are 
included in this contract modification #2 request.

Dear Mr. Ferreira: 
In accordance with your electronic mail request, Ninyo & Moore is pl eased to submit this proposal 
to perform a Preliminary Initial S ite Assessment (PISA), and Asbestos Containing Material (ACM) 
and Lead-Based Paint (LBP) Surveys for the planned sidewalk improvements  located along  
2nd North Avenue and 3 rd North Avenue, bet ween North Randall A venue and Westover Avenue  
(the Site). The project work involves improvements, such as sidewalks, and multi-use paths and 
crossings, to make walking and bic ycling to school safer and easier for students in Joseph City, a 
rural unincorporated community. The im provements will be ADA accessible. No new ri ght-of-way 
(ROW) is anticipated.  
The scope of services for this PISA, and ACM and LBP Survey, is consistent with the expectations 
of Arizona Department of Transport ation Environmental & En forcement Group for the preparation 
of a PISA which includes an ACM and LB P Survey. The objective of this PISA is to evaluate 
whether properties within and adjacent to existing and proposed transportation improvements 
within the specified Site area pose sufficient risk of hazardous materials’ impact to warrant further 
investigative steps. 
Ninyo & Moore has prepared the following scope of services and fee quotation based on the 
request and information provided by Wilson & Company, Inc.

<!-- page 569 -->
Ninyo & Moore | Navajo County, Joseph City Sidewalk Improvements, 2nd and 3rd N. Ave, Joseph City, Arizona | 13PHX03-01179 | March 7, 2024 2 
 
SCOPE OF SERVICES 
PISA 
Ninyo & Moore's proposed scope of services for this PISA will include the activities listed below: 
• Perform a reconnaissance to visually evaluate the Site area for possibly contaminated surficial 
soil or surface water, improperly stored hazardous material s, possibl e sources of 
polychlorinated biphenyls , and possible risks of co ntamination from activities at ad jacent 
properties. 
• Review readily available regulatory agency databases for the Site and facilities located 
adjacent to the Site. The purpose of this  review is to evaluate the po ssible environmental 
impacts to the Site from properties listed on regulatory agency databases. Databases will 
evaluate locations of known hazardous waste generators, landfills, facilities with leaking 
underground storage tanks and/or underground storage t anks, and facilities that use, store, or 
dispose of hazardous materials. 
• Prepare a PISA  report, assessing current Site conditions, and documenting findings  and 
providing recommendations regarding whether further assessment of the Site is recommended. 
Color photographs will be provided in the report. 
The PISA is not intended to cover all aspects of a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment outlined 
in the ASTM International (ASTM) E1527 -21. Furthermore, the following represents addi tional  
out-of-scope items with respect to this PISA, and therefore , will not be addressed: radon, lead in 
drinking water, wetlands, regulatory compliance, cultural and historical risk, industrial hygiene, 
health and safety, ecological resources, endanger ed species, indoor air quality, and high -voltage 
power lines. In addition, Ninyo & Moore will not address interpretations of zoning regulations , 
building code requirements, or property title issues. 
ACM Survey 
Ninyo & Moore's proposed scope of services for  the ACM Survey w ill include the activities listed 
below: 
• The ACM su rvey will consist of a visual assessment of the Site  to identify homogeneous 
suspect ACMs (suspect ACM generally uniform in color, texture, construction or application 
date, and general appearance). Each homogeneous suspect ACM will be observed for material 
type, location, condition, and friability. 
• Following identification of homogenous s uspect ACM, Ninyo & Moore will collect bulk samples 
of suspect ACM from readily accessible areas repres entative of the features within the Site. 
Bulk samples will be collected in general accordance with Occupational Safety and Health 
Administration (OSHA), National Emission Standard for Hazardous Air Pollutants , and AHERA 
guidelines. The samples will be col lected in re- sealable plastic bags and labeled with uni que 
sample identification numbers.

<!-- page 570 -->
Ninyo & Moore | Navajo County, Joseph City Sidewalk Improvements, 2nd and 3rd N. Ave, Joseph City, Arizona | 13PHX03-01179 | March 7, 2024 3 
 
• Samples of suspect ACMs will be delivered to a laboratory accredited by the National Voluntary 
Laboratory Accreditation Program for bulk asbestos fiber analysis. 
• Ninyo & Moore will not dismantle roadway components due to accessibility and safety issues; 
therefore, unidentified asbestos may be present at the Site. Should renovation/demolition 
activities begin and suspect ACM be discovered in inaccessible features or othe r areas on the 
Site, the material should be evaluated for asbestos prior to disturbance. 
• Bulk samples will be analyzed for the presence and quantification of asbestos fibers using 
polarized light microscopy coupled with dispersion staining. 
• Ninyo & Moore will prepare an ACM and LBP S urvey report, as a stand-alone document, and 
not as an appendix to the PISA report . This report will present Ninyo  & Moore’s data and 
summarize Ninyo & Moore’s conclusions and recommendations regarding the analytical results 
for the ACM samples obtained from the Site . The report wil l describe f ield a ctivities and 
procedures, sample location documentation, and the analytical results. The report will contain 
analytical data tables, figures, laboratory reports, and chain of custody forms. 
LBP Survey 
Ninyo & Moore's proposed scope of work for the LBP Survey will include the following activities: 
• The purpose of the LBP Survey is to identify whether r oadway striping and other painted 
components within the Site  would be classified as LBP (EPA regulated in some structures) or 
lead-containing paint (OSHA regulated  for worker protection) . Paint chip samples  
(one from each color/substrate combination) will be collected and submitted f or laboratory 
analysis. Sa mple analysi s will be conducted  using United States Environ mental Protection 
Agency Test Method 6010B, or other approved method. 
• Upon receipt of the analytical results, the laboratory test data will be evaluated with respect to 
applicable regulatory thresholds. 
• Ninyo &  Moore will prepar e an ACM and LBP Survey report . This report will present  
Ninyo & Moore’s LBP data and summarize Ninyo & Moore’s conclusions and recommendations 
regarding the analytical results for the LBP samples obtained from the Site.  The report will 
describe field activities and procedures, sample location figure(s), and the laboratory report and 
chain of custody for m. The LBP s urvey report will include a discussion of applicable EPA and 
OSHA standards for protection of the environmental and workers during the p lanned 
disturbance of these materials. This discussion will include references to asbestos and lead in 
construction guidance documents, such as OSHA’s Lead in Cons truction Bulletin 3142. If any 
LBP, lead- containing paints , or lead- containing t runcated dome pads ar e identified, then 
recommendations for OSHA -compliant practices to reduce or eliminate airborne lead dust  
generation during construction will be provided.

ASSUMPTIONS 
The proposed fee is based on the scope of services presented above and Ninyo & Moore’s 
understanding of the existing conditions at the Site and the roadway to be assessed. The fee does 
not include additional laboratory analyses fees or costs that  may arise due to unforeseen or 
unfavorable conditions or for post -report consultations. The follow ing assumptions were made in 
the development of this proposal: 
• Wilson & Company, Inc. will provide access to the Site for Ninyo & Moore personnel, including 
existing ROW. 
• Approximately 24 bulk samples will be collected and analyzed for asbestos content. 
• Approximately 18 paint chip samples will be collected and analyzed for lead content. 
• The laboratory analyses fees and other associated costs are included within this scope of work. 
Should additional laboratory analyses be requested, Ninyo & Moore will submi t a change order 
for approval by Wilson & Company, Inc. prior to authorizing the additional analysis. 
• No traffic control measures will be needed for this project.  
• Ninyo & Moore will not need to obtain any environmental clearance as a part of this project.  
SCHEDULE 
Ninyo & Moore estimates the proposed services can be completed within approximately six weeks 
of receipt of written notice to proceed and permission for access to the Site.

understanding of the project. Any additional services, not included in the aforementioned scope,

In performing environmental, hydrologic, or hydrogeologic services, CONSULTANT may excavate or otherwise come in 
contact with hazardous materials. CLIENT represents that CLIENT has informed CONSULTANT of the presence of any known 
hazardous materials. 
CLIENT recognizes that a project site containing hazardous materials may not perform as anticipated by CLIENT, even though 
CONSULTANT's services are performed with currently acceptable levels of care and skill. Further, CLIENT acknowledges 
that, while necessary for site exploration, commonly used exploration methods such as drilling borings and excavating 
trenches involve an inherent risk. For example, exploration on a project site containing contaminated materials may result in 
inducing cross-contamination and/or other negative effects. 
Unanticipated hazardous materials may be encountered in an area where there is no reason to believe they could or should 
be present. CONSULTANT and CLIENT agree that the discovery of unanticipated hazardous materials may make it necessary 
for CONSULTANT to take immediate measures to protect health and safety. CLIENT agrees to compensate CONSULTANT 
for any equipment decontamination or other costs arising out of the discovery of hazardous materials. 
CONSULTANT agrees to notify CLIENT when hazardous materials or suspected hazardous materials are encountered. 
CLIENT agrees to make any disclosures required by law to the appropriate governing agencies. CLIENT also agrees to hold 
CONSULTANT harmless for  any and all consequences of disclosures made by CONSULTANT which are required by 
governing law. In the event that the project site is not owned by CLIENT, CLIENT recognizes that it is CLIENT's responsibility 
to inform the property owner of the discovery of hazardous materials or suspected hazardous materials. 
Notwithstanding any other provision of the AGREEMENT, CLIENT waives any claim against CONSULTANT and, to the 
maximum extent permitted by law, agrees to defend, indemnify, and save CONSULTANT harmless from any claim, liability, 
and/or defense cost for injury or loss arising from CONSULTANT's discovery of hazardous materials or suspected hazardous 
materials, including, but not limited to, any costs created by delay of development projects and any cost as sociated with 
possible reduction of the property's value. 
CLIENT will be solely responsible for the ultimate disposal of any materials secured by CONSULTANT which are found to be 
contaminated. Such materials include, but are not limited to, drilling mud, soil, groundwater, and other materials removed from 
excavations. Contaminated materials will be placed in suitable storage containers, labeled, and left on site. 
SAMPLE DISPOSAL 
CONSULTANT will dispose of soil, rock, and water samples collected for analyses approximately thirty (30) days after the 
laboratory analysis report date. Further storage or transfer of samples can be made at CLIENT's expense upon CLIENT's 
prior written request. 
OWNERSHIP AND MAINTENANCE OF DOCUMENTS 
Unless otherwise specified in this Agreement or in an Addendum, and provided that CONSULTANT has been fully paid for 
the Services, CLIENT shall have the right to use the documents, maps, photographs, drawings and specifications resulting 
from CONSULTANT’s efforts on the project, for purposes reasonably contemplated by the parties. CONSULTANT shall have 
the right, but shall not be obligated, to retain copies of all such materials and shall have the right to use the same for an y 
purpose, unless such use would be expected to cause harm to CLIENT. CLIENT shall specify in advance, in writing, and be 
charged for all arrangements for special or extended- period maintenance of such materials by CONSULTANT. 
CONSULTANT retains the right of ownership with respect to any patentable concepts or copyrightable materials arising from 
its Services. 
Reuse of any material described by CLIENT, including publication to third parties, on extension of this project or on any other 
project without CONSULTANT’s written authorization, shall be at CLIENT’s risk, and CLIENT agrees to indemnify, defend, 
and hold harmless CONSULTANT from all claims, damages, and expenses, including attorney’s fees, arising out of such 
unauthorized reuse.

BILLING AND PAYMENT 
CLIENT will pay CONSULTANT in accordance with the procedures indicated in the Proposal and its attachments. Invoices 
will be submitted to CLIENT by CONSULTANT, and will be due and payable upon presentation. If CLIENT objects to all or 
any portion of any invoice, CLIENT will so notify CONSULTANT in writing within fourteen (14) calendar days of the invoice 
date, identify the cause of disagreement, and pay when due that portion of the invoice not in dispute. The parties will 
immediately make every effort to settle the disputed portion of the invoice. In the absence of written notification described 
above, the balance as stated on the invoice will be paid. 
Invoices are delinquent if payment has not been received within thirty (30) days from date of invoice. CLIENT will pay an 
additional charge of three quarters of a percent (.75) per month (or the maximum percentage allowed by law, whichever is 
lower) on any delinquent amount, excepting any portion of the invoiced amount in dispute and resolved in favor of CLIENT.  
Payment thereafter will first be applied to accrued interest and then to the principal unpaid amount. All time spent and expenses 
incurred (including any attorney's fees) in connection with collection of any delinquent amount will be paid by CLIENT to 
CONSULTANT per CONSULTANT's current fee schedules. In the event CLIENT fails to pay CONSULTANT within sixty (60) 
days after invoices are rendered, CLIENT agrees that CONSULTANT will have the right to consider the failure to pay the 
CONSULTANT's invoice as a breach of this AGREEMENT and CONSULTANT may cease work on the proje ct. At 
CONSULTANT’s option, CONSULTANT may waive said major breach upon payment by CLIENT of all arrearages and 
outstanding invoices. 
TERMINATION 
This AGREEMENT may be terminated by either party seven (7) days after written notice in the event of any breach of any 
provision of this AGREEMENT or in the event of substantial failure of performance by either party, or if CLIENT suspends the 
work for more than three (3) months. In the event of termination, CONSULTANT will be paid for services performed prior to 
the date of termination plus reasonable termination expenses, including, but not limited to, the cost of completing analyses, 
records, and reports necessary to document job status at the time of termination. 
RISK ALLOCATION 
Many risks potentially affect CONSULTANT by virtue of entering into this AGREEMENT to perform professional consulting 
services on behalf of CLIENT. The principal risk is the potential for human error by CONSULTANT. For CLIENT to obtain the 
benefit of a fee which includes a nominal allowance for dealing with CONSULTANT's liability, CLIENT agrees to limit 
CONSULTANT's liability to CLIENT and to all other parties for claims arising out of CONSULTANT's performance of the 
services described in this AGREEMENT. The aggregate liability of CONSULT ANT will not exceed $50,000 for negligent 
professional acts, errors, or omissions, including attorney’s fees and costs which may be awarded to the prevailing party, and 
CLIENT agrees to indemnify and hold harmless CONSULTANT from and against all liabilities in excess of the monetary limit 
established above. 
Limitations on liability and indemnities in this AGREEMENT are business understandings between the parties voluntarily and 
knowingly entered into, and shall apply to all theories of recovery including, but not limited to, breach of contract, warranty, 
tort (including negligence), strict or statutory liability, or any other cause of action, except for willful misconduct or gr oss 
negligence. The parties also agree that CLIENT will not seek damages in excess of the limitations indirectly through suits with 
other parties who may join CONSULTANT as a third-party defendant. Parties means CLIENT and CONSULTANT and their 
officers, employees, agents, affiliates, and subcontractors. 
Both CLIENT and CONSULTANT agree that they will not be liable to each other, under any circumstances, for special, indirect, 
consequential, or punitive damages arising out of or related to this AGREEMENT. 
INDEMNIFICATION 
If any claim is brought against CONSULTANT, its employees, agents and subcontractors and/or CLIENT by a third party, 
relating in any way to the Services, the contribution and indemnification rights and obligations of CONSULTANT and Client, 
subject to the paragraph titled “Risk Allocation” above, such claim shall be determined as follows: 
1. If any negligence, breach of contract, or willful misconduct of CONSULTANT caused any damage, injury, or loss 
claimed by the third party, then CONSULTANT and CLIENT shall each indemnify the other against any loss or 
judgement on a comparative negligence basis (CLIENT responsibility to include that of its agents, employees, and 
other contractors); and

caused the damage, injury, or loss asserted in the third party claim, CLIENT shall indemnify CONSULTANT against

DISPUTE RESOLUTION 
If a dispute at law arises from matters related to the services provided under this AGREEMENT and that dispute requires 
litigation, then: 
1. The claim will be brought and tried in judicial jurisdiction of the court of the county where CONSULTANT's principal

2. The prevailing party will be entitled to recovery of all reasonable costs incurred, including staff time, court costs,
attorneys' and expert witness fees, and other claim-related expenses
GOVERNING LAW AND SURVIVAL 
If any of the provisions contained in this AGREEMENT are held illegal, invalid, or unenforceable, the enforceability of the 
remaining provisions will not be impaired. Risk allocation and indemnities will survive termination or failure of this 
AGREEMENT for any cause.

Title: Amendment No. 1 to Contract No. B23-01-009 Navajo County Multimodal Transportation
Planning Study
Submitted For: Madhav Mundle, Public Works Director 
Submitted By: Jeanine Carruthers, Deputy Director Administration
Department: Public Works
Motion before the Board:
Amendment Number 1 to Contract No. B23-01-009 Navajo County Multimodal Transportation Planning
Study extends the contract with Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. one additional year (April 25, 2024 -
April 24, 2025)
Background:
On April 25, 2023 the Board of Supervisors awarded Contract No. B23-01-009 Navajo County Regional
Multimodal Transportation Planning Study to Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc.  This project will
perform Navajo County’s regional multimodal transportation planning study on the 16-mile segment of
SR 260 between US 60 and SR 73 and the surrounding neighborhoods.   The project will identify areas
for improvement, determine adequate safety measures, and will examine safety issues affecting
pedestrians, bicyclists, non-motorized users, and their interactions with motorized users. The project will
develop an active multimodal transportation plan that guides Navajo County to increase mobility and
community connectivity with adequate transportation facilities, including ADA compliant facilities, and
public transit services. The planning study will explore innovative technologies to address pedestrian and
bicycle safety issues affecting a rural community.  Amendment No. 1 of this contract extends the term
one additional year (April 25, 2024 - April 24, 2025).

RE: Conductor Replacement – Enhancing Energy Resilience in Arizona Communities 
 
Dear Mr. Traver,  
 
The Navajo County Board of Supervisors are pleased to offer our full support to Arizona Public 
Service Company (“APS”) in their program titled Conductor Replacement – Enhancing Energy 
Resilience in Arizona Communities. This program is being proposed to the Department of Energy 
(DOE) under the Grid Resilience Innovative Partnerships (GRIP) Program Funding Opportunity 
Announcement (FOA) Number: DE-FOA-0003195. Through this program, APS will be able to 
replace existing conductors that have reached the end of their design lives. Replacing identified aged 
conductors will increase reliability for customers and increase resiliency of the grid against extreme 
weather. 
 
Through the support of DOE funding, APS will significantly strengthen the grid’s capacity to 
withstand the increased grid load, extreme weather events, and ensure a resilient and dependable 
energy supply for Arizona. By systematically replacing aged conductors, APS significantly enhances 
reliability for 48,000 customers. This initiative also fortifies the grid’s resilience, while translating to 
long-term cost savings by averting emergency repairs and aligns with eco-friendly practices while 
integrating innovative technologies. It is clear to Navajo County that this project will provide 
economic and quality-of-life enhancing benefits to the people and communities of Arizona.  
 
Navajo County is well positioned for economic growth over the next five to ten years but that cannot 
be achieved without a reliable electrical grid.  Through APS’ initiative to replace conductors, they 
will ensure our grid is not only reliable but safe and can support continued growth. 
 
Navajo County is hopeful to see the successful completion of this project through award to APS, and 
thanks the DOE for the opportunity to provide funding to APS to bring this important project to life.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
Jason E. Whiting, Chairman 
Navajo County Board of Supervisors
